Models generate full option text evaluated using exact match (EM), BLEU, ROUGE (R1/R2/RL), and BERTScore (P/R/F1). All metrics reported as percentages. ↑ indicates higher is better. Baseline uses no encryption (plaintext). Best performing encryption method per configuration in bold.

Table 11. Training stability analysis across four random seeds. Results span baseline (plaintext), fully secured (FS+OU), and HERALD (PS+OU) configurations with three representative cryptographic methods (AES (SIV), Blowfish (ECB), FPE). All configurations exhibit low variance (coefficient of variation < 0.60%), with standard deviations ranging from 0.19–0.30 percentage points. CV = Coefficient of Variation.

Figure 2. Comparison of HERALD with a traditional pipeline. (i) Traditional: plaintext clinical notes are sent to a remote model, exposing sensitive content. (ii) HERALD: sensitive spans are encrypted on-device into tokens (shown in red); the server processes only the transformed input and the client decodes outputs locally. Observers see only unreadable strings for protected tokens, while task utility is preserved.
Table 18. Performance comparison of marker schemes for encrypted token delimitation.

Figure 3. Text variants used in our MCQ experiments. (A) Unsecured base multiple-choice question. (B) FS+OU: the question stem is fully secured, while the answer options remain in plaintext (“options unsecured”). (C) FS+OFS: both stem and options are fully secured. (D) PS+OU: the stem is partially secured using HERALD; options remain in plaintext. (E) PS+OPS: both stem and options are partially secured with HERALD. These controlled variants allow us to measure model performance under increasing degrees of semantic obfuscation.

Figure 5. Utility under full vs. selective security. Radar plots report test F1 for ClinicalBERT/Med-TC, Llama-3.1-Aloe-Beta8B/MedMCQA, and Qwen-2.5-7B/MedQA-USMLE. The outer green ring is plaintext; inner polygons compare FS (all tokens secured) with HERALD (PS). For MCQ, options are either plaintext (OU) or secured (OFS/OPS).
Table 14. Preprocessing for all secured methods. Lower ms/example is better; higher MB/s is better. n=200 examples. Results are shown with cache (✓) and without cache (×).

Figure 6. Attention mapping under varying security regimes. We visualize token-wise incoming attention at Layer 16 (of 32), averaged over heads. Panels: (A) Base, (B) FS+OU (fully secured stem; plaintext options), (C) FS+OFS (fully secured stem and options), (D) HERALD PS+OU (partially secured stem; plaintext options), and (E) HERALD PS+OPS (partially secured stem and options). In (D–E), spans wrapped by #^ ... ^# are HERALD-encrypted blocks; in (B–C), all tokens (and options in C) are directly transformed. Rendering: darker brown, larger boxes denote higher attention to that token; smaller, darker purple boxes denote lower attention.

Table 21. Regurgitation probes. EM: exact match; MS: mean similarity (0–1); CMR: ciphertext-marker rate. Free-form recall fails (EM=0), and HERALD always emits ciphertext in such cases (CMR=1.0). Long-prefix continuation yields high EM for both models, including TEST, indicating anchored completion rather than train-specific memorization; HERALD transitions into ciphertext when continuations touch sensitive spans. Values are averaged over multiple runs.
